Livagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala) is a synthetic tetrapeptide bioregulator studied for its effects on peptidase inhibition and epigenetic modulation in aging tissues [1] [4] . Preclinical research demonstrates Livagen strongly inhibits enkephalin-degrading enzymes [1] and induces heterochromatin decondensation with gene reactivation in aged cells [4] . No standardized human dosing exists; this educational protocol presents a once-daily subcutaneous approach based on analogy with similar peptide bioregulators. 06 Protocol Overview Concise summary of the once-daily regimen. Goal: Support cellular homeostasis and regenerative processes in aging tissues [3] . Schedule: Daily subcutaneous injections for 8–12 weeks (extend to 16 weeks if desired). Dose Range: 0.5–2.0 mg daily with gradual titration. Reconstitution: 3.0 mL per 20 mg vial (~6.67 mg/mL) for accurate unit measurements. Storage: Lyophilized frozen; reconstituted refrigerated; avoid repeated freeze–thaw. 07 Dosing Protocol Suggested daily titration approach. Start: 0.5 mg daily; increase by ~0.5 mg every 1–2 weeks as tolerated. Target: 1.5–2.0 mg daily by Weeks 5–12. Frequency: Once per day (subcutaneous). Cycle Length: 8–12 weeks; optional extension to 16 weeks. Timing: Any consistent time; rotate injection sites. 08 Storage Instructions Proper storage preserves peptide quality. Lyophilized: Store at −20 °C (−4 °F) in dry, dark conditions; minimize moisture exposure. Reconstituted: Refrigerate at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F); prepare aliquots if needed and avoid freeze–thaw . Allow vials to reach room temperature before opening to reduce condensation uptake. 09 Important Notes Practical considerations for consistency and safety. Use new sterile insulin syringes; dispose in a sharps container [5] . Rotate injection sites (abdomen, thighs, upper arms) to reduce local irritation [6] . Inject slowly; wait a few seconds before withdrawing the needle. Document daily dose and site rotation to maintain consistency. No standardized human clinical administration studies exist for Livagen; dosing is extrapolated from preclinical data and similar peptide bioregulators. 10 How This Works Livagen’s mechanisms involve peptidase inhibition and epigenetic modulation. The peptide strongly inhibits enkephalin-degrading enzymes (IC50 ≈ 20 μM) in human serum [1] , which may prolong endogenous enkephalin activity. Notably, this occurs without direct opioid receptor binding [1] . In aging cells, Livagen has been shown to induce heterochromatin decondensation and reactivate ribosomal genes [4] . Preclinical studies in rat liver organ cultures demonstrated enhanced cellular structure and regenerative processes [3] , while oral administration in aged rats shifted digestive enzyme activities toward youthful patterns [2] . 11 Potential Benefits & Side Effects Observations from preclinical and in vitro literature. Supports inhibition of enkephalin-degrading enzymes, potentially prolonging endogenous enkephalin signaling [1] . May modulate gene expression and chromatin structure in aging tissues [4] . Preclinical evidence suggests support for cellular homeostasis and regenerative capacity [3] . In aged rodents, oral dosing normalized digestive enzyme activity toward youthful levels [2] . No human clinical administration studies have been reported; side effect profile in humans is unknown. Occasional mild injection-site reactions (redness/itch) may occur with subcutaneous administration. 12 Lifestyle Factors Complementary strategies for best outcomes. Maintain a balanced, nutrient-dense diet to support cellular health. Engage in regular physical activity to reinforce metabolic and regenerative adaptations. Prioritize sleep quality and stress management to support overall homeostasis. 13 Injection Technique General subcutaneous guidance from clinical best-practice resources [7] . Clean the vial stopper and skin with alcohol; allow to dry [6] . Pinch a skinfold; insert the needle at 45–90° into subcutaneous tissue [6] [8] . Do not aspirate for subcutaneous injections; inject slowly and steadily [9] . Rotate sites systematically (abdomen, thighs, upper arms) to avoid lipohypertrophy [6] . Dispose of used syringes immediately in a sharps container [5] . 14 Important Note This content is intended for therapeutic educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. 15 References 1 Biology Bulletin (Springer) - Effects of Livagen and Epitalon on Enkephalin-Degrading Enzymes from Human Serum View Source 2 PubMed - Effect of peptide Livagen on activity of digestive enzymes in gastrointestinal tract and non-digestive organs in rats of different ages View Source 3 PubMed - Functional morphology of an organotypic liver culture exposed to the peptide Livagen View Source 4 ResearchGate / Neuroendocrinology Letters - Peptides and Ageing: heterochromatin decondensation and gene reactivation View Source 5 CDC - Preventing Unsafe Injection Practices (clinical safety and sharps disposal) View Source 6 MedlinePlus - Subcutaneous (SQ) injections: technique, site rotation, and skin preparation View Source 7 PMC - Subcutaneous Drug Injection Review: pharmacologic considerations of the subcutaneous route View Source 8 CDC (Subcut Injection PDF) - Vaccine Administration: Subcutaneous injection technique and site guidance View Source 9 Immunize.org - How to Administer Intramuscular and Subcutaneous Vaccine Injections (no aspiration guidance) View Source 11 Pure Lab Peptides - Livagen (20 mg) product page (quality and batch documentation) View Source Additional Research and Background These sources provide related context and are not presented as support for a specific statement above. 1 NCBI Bookshelf - Best practices for injection: asepsis, preparation, and administration View Source 16 Related research, protocols, and guides Explore the available research context, protocol variants or comparisons, and practical guides. LL-37 (also known as CAP-18) is a 37-amino-acid cationic antimicrobial peptide derived from the C-terminal of human cathelicidin (hCAP18) [1] . It is the only known human cathelicidin, exhibiting broad-spectrum antibacterial activity and immune-modulating properties [2] [3] . This educational protocol presents a once-daily subcutaneous approach using a practical dilution for clear insulin-syringe measurements. 06 Protocol Overview Concise summary of the once-daily regimen. Goal: Support antimicrobial defense and wound-healing processes [4] [5] . Schedule: Daily subcutaneous injections for 8–12 weeks (extend to 16 weeks if desired). Dose Range: 50–400 µg daily with gradual titration. Reconstitution: 3.0 mL per 5 mg vial (~1.67 mg/mL) for accurate unit measurements. Storage: Lyophilized frozen; reconstituted refrigerated; avoid repeated freeze–thaw. 07 Dosing Protocol Suggested daily titration approach. Start: 50–100 µg daily; increase by ~50 µg each week as tolerated. Target: 200–400 µg daily by Weeks 4–8. Frequency: Once per day (subcutaneous); optional 5-on/2-off schedule. Cycle Length: 8–12 weeks; optional extension to 16 weeks. Timing: Any consistent time; rotate injection sites. 08 Storage Instructions Proper storage preserves peptide quality [6] . Lyophilized: Store at −20 °C (−4 °F) in dry, dark conditions; follow the product’s validated shelf life. Reconstituted: Refrigerate at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F); do not infer a use-by period or freezing extension without stability data for the exact formulation. Allow vials to reach room temperature before opening to reduce condensation uptake. 09 Important Notes Practical considerations for consistency and safety. Use new sterile insulin syringes; dispose in a sharps container [8] . Rotate injection sites (abdomen, thighs, upper arms) to reduce local irritation [9] . Inject slowly; wait a few seconds before withdrawing the needle. Document daily dose and site rotation to maintain consistency. Early-phase doses (≤10 units) benefit from 30- or 50-unit syringes for precision. 10 How This Works LL-37 exerts both direct and indirect antimicrobial effects. Its amphipathic, cationic α-helical structure (net +6 charge) allows it to preferentially bind and disrupt negatively charged microbial membranes [2] . Beyond direct killing, LL-37 modulates host immunity: in murine sepsis models, it induced neutrophils to release microvesicles rich in antimicrobial proteins, lowering bacterial burden and improving survival [3] . LL-37 can also bind bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and block its interaction with CD14/TLR4, reducing endotoxin-triggered TNF release and neutrophil apoptosis [2] . These combined mechanisms help explain its potential in infection control and tissue-repair contexts. 11 Potential Benefits & Side Effects Observations from preclinical and clinical literature. In chronic venous leg ulcers (which often lack endogenous LL-37), topical treatment with synthetic LL-37 significantly accelerated healing rates compared to placebo [4] . In diabetic foot ulcer trials, LL-37 cream improved granulation tissue formation and wound closure [5] . Broad-spectrum antimicrobial action helps clear infections; in experimental sepsis models, LL-37 treatment reduced bacterial loads and mortality [3] . Generally well tolerated; occasional mild injection-site reactions (redness, itch) may occur with subcutaneous administration. 12 Lifestyle Factors Complementary strategies for best outcomes. Optimize vitamin D status, as vitamin D upregulates endogenous cathelicidin/LL-37 expression [10] . Support wound healing with adequate protein intake and micronutrient sufficiency (zinc, vitamin C). Maintain proper wound hygiene and dressing protocols if using for tissue-repair goals. Prioritize sleep and stress management to support immune function and recovery. 13 Injection Technique General subcutaneous guidance from clinical best-practice resources [11] . Clean the vial stopper and skin with alcohol; allow to dry. Pinch a skinfold; insert the needle at 45–90° into subcutaneous tissue [9] [12] . Do not aspirate for subcutaneous injections; inject slowly and steadily [12] . Rotate sites systematically (abdomen, thighs, upper arms) and move at least 2–3 cm from the previous site [9] . Mazdutide, also called IBI362 or LY3305677, is a once-weekly dual GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist studied in adults with obesity, overweight, and type 2 diabetes. Randomized phase 1b, phase 2, and phase 3 trials evaluated different populations, dose levels, and durations; those studies do not establish that an independently supplied research vial is interchangeable with a clinical-trial formulation. [1] [2] [3] [4] 06 Protocol Overview Concise summary of the once‑weekly regimen. Goal: Support chronic weight management and metabolic improvement through dual GLP‑1/glucagon receptor activation. [2] [3] Schedule: Once‑weekly subcutaneous injections for 8–12 weeks minimum (clinical trials ranged from 12–48 weeks). Dose Range: 2.5–5 mg weekly with gradual titration; advanced protocols may reach 10 mg. Reconstitution: 3.0 mL per 10 mg vial (~3.33 mg/mL) for standard dosing; 2.0 mL for higher concentrations if needed. Storage: Lyophilized frozen at −20 °C (−4 °F); reconstituted refrigerated at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F); follow the exact product’s validated use-by date. 07 Dosing Protocol Suggested weekly titration approach. Start: 2.5 mg once weekly for first 4 weeks to establish tolerability. Increase: Advance to 5 mg weekly at week 5; maintain for remainder of protocol (weeks 5–12+). Frequency: Once per week (subcutaneous injection). Cycle Length: Minimum 8 weeks; clinical evidence supports 12–48 week protocols. Timing: Administer on the same day each week; rotate injection sites to avoid irritation. 08 Storage Instructions Proper storage preserves peptide stability and potency. Lyophilized: Store at −20 °C (−4 °F) or below in dry, dark conditions; protect from moisture. Reconstituted: Refrigerate at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F); bacteriostatic water does not establish peptide stability or a universal use-by period. Important: Do not freeze reconstituted solution; avoid freeze–thaw cycles which can denature the peptide. Discard: Follow the specific product’s validated use-by period. Discard if cloudiness or particulates appear. 09 Mazdutide Dose and 10 mg Vial Math A 10 mg vial mixed with 3.0 mL contains about 3.33 mg of mazdutide per mL. On a U-100 syringe, 1 unit marks 0.01 mL, so each unit represents about 0.0333 mg, or 33.3 mcg. The primary mazdutide dosage table above keeps peptide mass, syringe units, milliliters, frequency, and duration together so each row can be interpreted without a separate calculator. Concentration: 10 mg ÷ 3.0 mL = approximately 3.33 mg/mL. U-100 conversion: 3.33 mg/mL × 0.01 mL per unit = approximately 0.0333 mg per unit. Volume check: milligrams ÷ 3.33 mg/mL = milliliters; milliliters × 100 = U-100 units. Vial limit: calculations cannot exceed the 10 mg total mass contained in one vial. Published clinical trials used manufactured study products under protocol-controlled conditions. Vial arithmetic can translate concentration and volume, but it cannot establish bioequivalence, sterility, stability, or an appropriate dose for any individual. [14] 10 Mazdutide Dosing in Phase 2 and Phase 3 Clinical Research Mazdutide dosing has differed across phase 1b, phase 2, and phase 3 research. Early randomized studies evaluated multiple once-weekly dose levels and escalation designs in adults with overweight or obesity and in patients with type 2 diabetes. [1] [12] [13] A phase 2 trial in Chinese adults with overweight or obesity studied 3 mg, 4.5 mg, and 6 mg dose groups over 24 weeks. [2] A separate phase 2 diabetes trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of mazdutide in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes. [4] Later work expanded the evidence base. GLORY-1 studied 4 mg and 6 mg in Chinese adults with overweight or obesity for 48 weeks. [3] A United States phase 2 clinical trial evaluated groups assigned to 3–6 mg, 10 mg, or 16 mg escalation targets in a diverse population. [6] [14] Separate research evaluated a 9 mg target in phase 2 and GLORY-2 phase 3 programs. [7] [8] A phase 1b study of mazdutide and later controlled trials assigned participants to different dose groups. Some research included 6 mg mazdutide, 9 mg and 10 mg targets, and a 16 mg mazdutide target under protocol-controlled escalation. These are study-specific doses of mazdutide, not a universal mazdutide dose. Trial population, formulation, escalation rules, monitoring, duration, and jurisdiction all matter. The locked chart above remains a calculation display for this 10 mg vial and has not been changed by the clinical evidence review. 11 Mazdutide for Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes: Dual Receptor Action Mazdutide is a dual GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist. GLP-1 receptor agonist activity is associated with glucose-dependent insulin signaling, delayed gastric emptying, and appetite-related effects. Glucagon receptor activity can influence hepatic energy metabolism and energy expenditure. Researchers are studying whether combined receptor activity produces a different metabolic profile from single-receptor medicines. [5] [11] Mechanism does not predict an individual response. A laboratory calculation also does not show whether the reconstituted material matches the composition, exposure, or quality controls of the product used in a clinical trial. For that reason, clinical outcomes and safety observations must remain tied to the studied population and formulation. 12 Body Weight Change and Waist Circumference Outcomes Randomized trials reported body weight change from baseline, body weight and waist circumference, glycemic markers, lipids, and other cardiometabolic outcomes. Participants receiving mazdutide were compared with placebo or active-control groups according to each protocol. The phase 2 obesity study found greater mean body weight reduction with mazdutide than placebo at the studied endpoints, while the phase 2 diabetes trial reported changes in HbA1c and body weight in patients with type 2 diabetes. [2] [4] In GLORY-1, adults with overweight or obesity assigned to mazdutide had greater reductions in body weight from baseline than those assigned to placebo at 48 weeks. The proportion of participants achieving weight-loss thresholds was also reported, but achieving weight loss in a trial does not predict an individual outcome. [3] The United States phase 2 study also reported body weight loss across evaluated dose groups, but the size and precision of an effect depend on the trial design and population. [6] Across different mazdutide doses, published research reported dose-dependent body weight reduction in some analyses. That does not define an optimal mazdutide dose, because tolerability, trial design, and population differed. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses combine several trials and can strengthen estimates of average efficacy and safety, but they also inherit differences among the included studies. Recent analyses found body weight reduction and metabolic changes across randomized controlled trials while noting heterogeneity and the need for longer follow-up. [9] [10] These findings describe groups, not guaranteed results. 13 Efficacy and Safety of Mazdutide: Evidence Limits Across clinical research, gastrointestinal events such as nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, reduced appetite, and abdominal symptoms were among the most commonly reported adverse events. Frequency and severity varied by dose, escalation design, population, and study duration. Higher doses of mazdutide were evaluated only within controlled protocols, and their safety profiles cannot be inferred from vial strength alone. [1] [2] [3] Dual agonist activity makes cardiovascular, gallbladder, pancreatic, hepatic, renal, and glycemic monitoring relevant in controlled research. Trial eligibility rules excluded some higher-risk groups, so the evidence does not automatically extend to every population. Published averages also do not rule out rare or delayed events. Meta-analyses support an overall summary of observed safety but cannot replace product-specific quality testing or medical oversight. [5] [9] [10] This page is educational and presents research calculations. It does not recommend treatment with mazdutide, diagnose a condition, or establish that any research product is suitable for human use. 14 Regulatory Status and Study Context The development of mazdutide includes obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes programs. Regulatory status varies by jurisdiction. Innovent reported that China’s National Medical Products Administration approved mazdutide for adult long-term weight control and for glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. [15] That authorization does not establish approval in the United States or every other country, and it does not validate independently supplied research material. The names IBI362 and LY3305677 appear in trial records and publications. ClinicalTrials.gov identifies the United States phase 2 study as NCT06124807 and provides its protocol-level eligibility, intervention, and outcome details. [14] Readers should check the current regulator and trial registry for the jurisdiction and study in question. 15 Storage, Handling, and Product Provenance The four reconstitution checks and temperature language in the primary chart are preserved exactly. A concentration calculation does not establish chemical stability or a universal discard period. Follow the exact label and validated lot-specific instructions for the product being handled. The linked Pure Lab Peptides page identifies the pictured 10 mg research vial and supports supplier and product provenance only. [16] It is not used as scientific evidence for clinical efficacy, safety, or trial dosing. 16 Mazdutide Dosage FAQs What concentration does a 10 mg vial make with 3.0 mL? It makes approximately 3.33 mg/mL. On a U-100 syringe, 1 unit equals 0.01 mL and therefore represents about 33.3 mcg at this concentration. Is a U-100 syringe unit a peptide unit? No. U-100 units are volume markings. The peptide amount depends on the vial mass and final reconstitution volume. What mazdutide dose did clinical trials study? Clinical research evaluated multiple once-weekly dose levels and escalation targets, including phase 2 and phase 3 programs. A trial dose is specific to its protocol and should not be converted into a universal recommendation. [6] [7] [8] Is mazdutide the same as a single GLP-1 receptor agonist? No. Mazdutide is designed as a dual GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist. That mechanism and its evidence base should not be treated as interchangeable with a single-receptor compound. [11] Do body weight results predict an individual outcome? No. Trial results summarize groups under controlled conditions. Individual outcomes can differ, and research-vial calculations do not establish equivalence to clinical-trial products. Where can the research record be checked? Peer-reviewed publications and ClinicalTrials.gov provide study designs, populations, endpoints, and safety findings. Use a new sterile insulin syringe for each weekly injection; dispose in a proper sharps container. [9] Rotate injection sites weekly (abdomen, thighs, upper arms) to minimize local irritation and lipoatrophy. [8] [10] For doses requiring >3 mL volume, split into two separate injections at different sites for comfort and absorption. Allow reconstituted vials to reach room temperature before withdrawing dose to reduce viscosity. Document dose, injection site, and any side effects to track response and optimize protocol. 10 How This Works Mazdutide functions as a dual agonist at both GLP‑1 and glucagon receptors, combining the appetite‑suppressing and glucose‑lowering effects of GLP‑1 with the energy‑expenditure benefits of glucagon activation. [2] [6] This dual mechanism distinguishes it from single‑target GLP‑1 agonists and has shown robust weight loss efficacy in clinical trials. Phase 2 studies demonstrated 6.7–11.3% body weight reduction at 3–6 mg weekly doses over 24 weeks. [2] A 48‑week phase 3 trial reported sustained weight loss of 11–14% with 4–6 mg weekly maintenance. [3] In type 2 diabetes populations, mazdutide achieved meaningful HbA1c reductions (~1.7%) alongside ~7% weight loss. [4] The extended half‑life enables convenient once‑weekly dosing with steady pharmacologic exposure. 11 Potential Benefits & Side Effects Observations from clinical trial evidence. Potential Benefits Significant body weight reduction (6–14% over 24–48 weeks) in obesity trials. [2] [3] [5] Meaningful HbA1c improvement (~1.7% reduction) in type 2 diabetes populations. [4] Favorable metabolic effects including improved lipid profiles and glucose control. Convenient once‑weekly dosing improves adherence compared to daily regimens. Common Side Effects Gastrointestinal effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation) are the most common adverse events, typically mild‑to‑moderate and diminishing with continued use. [5] Injection‑site reactions (redness, swelling, mild discomfort) may occur; rotate sites to minimize. Gradual dose titration significantly improves tolerability and reduces discontinuation rates. Prioritize consistent sleep (7–9 hours nightly) and stress management to support adherence and hormonal balance. [8] [10] Clean the vial stopper and injection site with alcohol swabs; allow to air‑dry completely. Use aseptic technique: wipe stoppers, use sterile needles, and avoid touching needle tip. Pinch a skinfold and insert the needle at 45–90° into subcutaneous fatty tissue (not muscle). Do not aspirate for subcutaneous injections; inject slowly and steadily over 5–10 seconds. Withdraw needle and apply gentle pressure with a clean swab; do not rub vigorously. Rotate injection sites systematically: abdomen (at least 2 inches from navel), front/outer thighs, or outer upper arms. It is not a universal dose and is not interchangeable with the later 16 mg afamelanotide implant. [2] [4] [7] 06 Melanotan I Human-Study Context Early human research evaluated a synthetic melanotropin analog by subcutaneous injection. [1] A pharmacokinetic study used 0.0363–0.0953 mg/lb (0.08–0.21 mg/kg) subcutaneously on five consecutive days for two weeks. [2] The chart uses only the lowest 0.0363 mg/lb (0.08 mg/kg) published amount and a clearly stated 154.3 lb (70 kg) arithmetic example. Later afamelanotide research used controlled implants rather than reconstituted injection vials. [4] [5] [6] Those implant studies are useful clinical context but are not formulation equivalents. 07 10 mg Vial and Weight-Based Calculation 10 mg divided by 1.0 mL equals 10 mg/mL . One U-100 unit equals 0.01 mL or 100 mcg . At 154.3 lb (70 kg), the published 0.0363 mg/lb (0.08 mg/kg) amount equals 5.6 mg . body: Home Single Peptide Dosages Melanotan II (10 mg Vial) Dosage Protocol Research reference · 10 mg vial Melanotan II (10 mg Vial) Dosage Protocol Written by PeptideDosages Editorial Team Published March 1, 2026 Updated September 20, 2026 Melanotan II is dosed at 250 mcg–1 mg daily via subcutaneous injection in educational protocols. A 10 mg vial reconstituted with bacteriostatic water yields about 3.33 mg/mL. This information is for research and educational use only. Keep this chart close Open this dosage and reconstitution chart directly from your account. Sign in to save 02 Melanotan II Dosage Chart Dosing & Reconstitution Guide Educational guide for reconstitution and daily dosing Standard / Gradual Titration (3 mL = 3.33 mg/mL) Week / Phase Daily Dose Units (per injection) (mL) Week 1 250 mcg (0.25 mg) 7.5 units (0.075 mL) Week 2 500 mcg (0.5 mg) 15 units (0.15 mL) Week 3 750 mcg (0.75 mg) 22.5 units (0.225 mL) Weeks 4–8 1000 mcg (1 mg) 30 units (0.30 mL) Maintenance (after Week 8) 500–1000 mcg (1–2× weekly) 15–30 units (0.15–0.30 mL) Frequency: Inject once daily subcutaneously during the initial 8-week tanning phase; transition to 1–2 injections per week for maintenance dosing to sustain pigmentation [3] . This schedule uses the standard 3.0 mL dilution for consistent unit measurements. For ≤10-unit (≤0.10 mL) administrations, consider 30- or 50-unit insulin syringes for improved readability. Reconstitution Steps Draw 3.0 mL bacteriostatic water with a sterile syringe. Inject slowly down the vial wall to avoid foaming; do not shake vigorously. Gently roll or swirl the vial until the powder is fully dissolved. Label the vial with the reconstitution date and store refrigerated at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F) , protected from light. Important: This guide is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Melanotan II is not an approved medication. For research use only. 03 Supplies Needed Plan based on an 8–16 week daily protocol with gradual titration (including transition to maintenance dosing). Peptide Vials (Melanotan II, 10 mg each): 8 weeks ≈ 5 vials (~45–50 mg total) 12 weeks ≈ 8 vials (~70–75 mg total) 16 weeks ≈ 10 vials (~95–100 mg total) Insulin Syringes (U-100, 1 mL): Per week (daily dosing): 7 syringes 8 weeks: 56 syringes 12 weeks: 84 syringes 16 weeks: 112 syringes Bacteriostatic Water (10 mL bottles): Use 3.0 mL per vial for reconstitution. 8 weeks (5 vials): 15 mL → 2 × 10 mL bottles 12 weeks (8 vials): 24 mL → 3 × 10 mL bottles 16 weeks (10 vials): 30 mL → 3 × 10 mL bottles Alcohol Swabs: One for the vial stopper + one for the injection site each day. Per week: 14 swabs (2/day) 8 weeks: 112 swabs → recommend 2 × 100-count boxes 12 weeks: 168 swabs → recommend 2 × 100-count boxes 16 weeks: 224 swabs → recommend 3 × 100-count boxes Melanotan II 10 mg View Supplier U-100 syringes View Supplier Bacteriostatic water View Supplier Alcohol swabs View Supplier 04 Peptide Reconstitution Simulator Practice preparing this vial with the verified strength and final volume from this protocol. × Exit simulator 05 Melanotan II Vial and Research Context Reconstitute: Add 3.0 mL bacteriostatic water → 3.33 mg/mL concentration. Typical daily range: 250–1000 mcg once daily (gradual titration over 8–12 weeks). Easy measuring: At 3.33 mg/mL, 1 unit = 0.01 mL ≈ 33.3 mcg on a U-100 insulin syringe. Storage: Lyophilized: freeze at −20 °C (−4 °F) or below; after reconstitution, refrigerate at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F) ; follow product-specific use-by instructions. Melanotan II is a synthetic analog of α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone studied for its ability to increase skin pigmentation and noted for inducing erectile activity as a side effect [1] . Early human trials identified effective daily doses in the range of 1–2 mg for tanning, with conservative protocols starting lower to minimize side effects such as nausea and flushing [3] . This educational protocol presents a once-daily subcutaneous titration approach using practical dilution for clear insulin-syringe measurements. 06 Protocol Overview Concise summary of the once-daily subcutaneous regimen. Goal: Increase skin pigmentation (tanning) through melanocortin receptor activation [1] . Schedule: Daily subcutaneous injections for 6–8 weeks during loading phase, then maintenance dosing 1–2× weekly [3] . Dose Range: 250–1000 mcg daily with gradual titration to minimize side effects. Reconstitution: 3.0 mL per 10 mg vial (3.33 mg/mL) for accurate unit measurements. Storage: Lyophilized frozen at −20 °C (−4 °F); reconstituted refrigerated at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F); follow product-specific use-by instructions. 07 Dosing Protocol Suggested daily titration approach based on clinical research. Start: 200–250 mcg daily; increase by 100–250 mcg increments every 1–2 weeks as tolerated. Target: 500–1000 mcg daily by Weeks 4–8 (studied effective range is 1–2 mg/day) [1] . Frequency: Once per day (subcutaneous) during loading phase. Cycle Length: 6–8 weeks for initial tanning, then switch to maintenance dosing. Maintenance: 500–1000 mcg administered 1–2× per week to sustain pigmentation [3] . Timing: Any consistent time; rotate injection sites to reduce irritation. 08 Storage Instructions Proper storage preserves peptide stability and potency. Lyophilized: Store at −20 °C (−4 °F) or below in dry, dark conditions; keep desiccated to minimize moisture exposure. Reconstituted: Refrigerate at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F); follow product-specific use-by and sterile-handling instructions; bacteriostatic water alone does not establish a shelf life. Avoid freeze–thaw: Do not refreeze reconstituted solution; do not assume aliquoting extends stability without validation. Allow vials to reach room temperature before opening to reduce condensation. 09 Important Notes Practical considerations for consistency and safety. Use new sterile insulin syringes for each injection; dispose in a sharps container immediately [9] . Rotate injection sites systematically (abdomen, thighs, upper arms) to reduce local irritation and scarring [10] . Clean vial stopper and injection site with alcohol swabs before each use; allow to air dry [11] . Inject slowly and steadily; wait a few seconds before withdrawing the needle. Document daily dose, injection site, and any side effects to maintain consistency and track tolerance. Safety warning: Do not exceed 2 mg per day; case reports document serious systemic toxicity and rhabdomyolysis at mega-doses (6 mg) [4] . 10 How This Works Melanotan II is a synthetic cyclic heptapeptide analog of α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone that binds to melanocortin receptors, particularly MC1R and MC4R [1] . Activation of MC1R on melanocytes stimulates melanin production and distribution, resulting in increased skin pigmentation even without UV exposure. Early Phase I studies in humans identified 0.025 mg/kg per day (approximately 1.5–2 mg for an average adult) as an appropriate dose, with measurable tanning observed after just five low doses administered over two weeks [1] . The peptide’s subcutaneous administration allows for steady melanocortin receptor activation, with effects accumulating over the course of daily injections during the initial tanning phase [3] . 11 Potential Benefits & Side Effects Observations from clinical trials and case reports. Potential Benefits Increases skin pigmentation (tanning) without UV exposure requirement [1] . Tanning effects observable after 5–10 daily injections in most individuals [1] . May induce spontaneous erections in men as a noted side effect (MC4R activation) [3] [5] . Maintenance dosing (1–2× weekly) can sustain pigmentation after initial loading phase [3] . Common Side Effects Nausea (dose-dependent; most common at higher doses) [1] . Facial flushing and increased skin warmth [3] . Reduced appetite and mild fatigue [1] . Spontaneous erections or increased libido in men [5] . Injection site reactions (redness, mild stinging) [9] . Serious Risks & Warnings Not FDA-approved: Melanotan II is not an approved medication; use carries regulatory and safety risks [6] . Dose-limiting toxicity: Severe sympathomimetic symptoms and rhabdomyolysis reported at 6 mg dose [4] . Mole changes: May alter pigmentation of existing moles; theoretical melanoma concerns warrant caution [6] . Cardiovascular effects: Transient increases in heart rate and blood pressure possible at higher doses [3] . 12 Lifestyle Factors Complementary strategies for safe and effective outcomes. UV exposure: Melanotan II increases melanin without UV, but some users combine with minimal UV exposure; always use appropriate sun protection to reduce skin cancer risk [6] . Hydration: Maintain adequate fluid intake, especially if experiencing nausea or appetite suppression. Monitoring: Inspect moles and skin regularly for changes; seek dermatological evaluation if new or changing lesions appear [6] . Dose discipline: Adhere strictly to conservative dosing protocols; never exceed 2 mg per day to avoid serious adverse effects [4] . 13 Injection Technique Subcutaneous injection guidance from clinical best-practice resources [9] [11] . Clean the vial stopper and injection site with alcohol swabs; allow both to air dry completely [11] . Use a 1 mL insulin syringe (29–31 gauge, ½ inch needle) for subcutaneous administration [9] . Pinch a fold of skin approximately 1 inch thick at the injection site (abdomen preferred, at least 2 inches from navel) [10] . Insert the needle at 45–90° depending on body composition; release the pinch after needle insertion [10] . Do not aspirate for subcutaneous injections; inject slowly and steadily [11] . Withdraw the needle at the same angle; apply gentle pressure with clean gauze if needed. Rotate sites systematically to avoid lipohypertrophy or scarring [10] . Dispose of used syringes immediately in a proper sharps container; never reuse needles [9] . 14 Important Note This content is intended for therapeutic educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Melanotan II is not an approved medication by the FDA or other regulatory agencies. Research use only; not for human consumption. Any use carries significant risks including potential serious adverse effects. Consult qualified healthcare professionals before considering any peptide research. 15 References 1 PubMed - Dorr RT et al. Mechano Growth Factor (MGF) is a splice variant of IGF‑1 (IGF‑1Ec in humans) produced in response to mechanical stress and tissue damage [1] [2] . Research indicates MGF plays a role in muscle repair, satellite cell activation, and bone regeneration [3] [4] . This educational protocol presents a once‑daily subcutaneous approach using a practical dilution for clear insulin‑syringe measurements. 06 Protocol Overview Concise summary of the once‑daily regimen. Goal: Support tissue repair and regenerative processes through localized growth factor signaling [3] [4] . Schedule: Daily subcutaneous injections for 8–12 weeks (extend to 16 weeks if desired). Dose Range: 100–300 mcg daily with gradual titration. Reconstitution: 3.0 mL per 5 mg vial (~1.67 mg/mL) for accurate unit measurements. Storage: Lyophilized frozen; reconstituted refrigerated; avoid repeated freeze–thaw. 07 Dosing Protocol Suggested daily titration approach. Start: 100 mcg daily; increase by ~50 mcg weekly as tolerated. Target: 250–300 mcg daily by Weeks 4–8. Frequency: Once per day (subcutaneous). Cycle Length: 8–12 weeks; optional extension to 16 weeks. Timing: Any consistent time; rotate injection sites. 08 Storage Instructions Proper storage preserves peptide quality. Lyophilized: Store at −20 °C (−4 °F) or colder for long‑term; refrigerate at 4 °C (39.2 °F) for short‑term. Reconstituted: Refrigerate at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F); follow the exact preparation’s validated use-by and sterile-handling instructions; avoid freeze–thaw cycles . Allow vials to reach room temperature before opening to reduce condensation uptake. 09 Important Notes Practical considerations for consistency and safety. Use new sterile insulin syringes; dispose in a sharps container. Rotate injection sites (abdomen, thighs, upper arms) to reduce local irritation [7] . Inject slowly; wait a few seconds before withdrawing the needle. Document daily dose and site rotation to maintain consistency. MGF has a short half‑life; PEGylated forms (PEG‑MGF) offer extended duration but follow different protocols [2] . 10 How This Works MGF is generated through alternative splicing of the IGF‑1 gene in response to mechanical loading or tissue injury [1] [2] . The resulting peptide contains a unique C‑terminal E domain that distinguishes it from systemic IGF‑1. Preclinical research demonstrates MGF activates satellite cells (muscle stem cells), promotes osteoblast proliferation, and supports neurogenesis [3] [4] [8] . These effects appear to be localized and transient, suggesting MGF acts primarily as a tissue‑specific repair signal rather than a systemic growth factor. 11 Potential Benefits & Side Effects Observations from preclinical literature (no formal human clinical trials have been completed). Promotes satellite cell activation and myoblast proliferation in muscle tissue [1] [9] . Supports bone defect healing and osteoblast activity in animal models [3] . May promote neurogenesis and neuroprotection in aging brain tissue [8] . Generally well tolerated in preclinical settings; occasional mild injection‑site reactions may occur with subcutaneous administration. Long‑term safety data in humans is limited; preclinical models suggest localized rather than systemic effects. 12 Lifestyle Factors Complementary strategies for best outcomes. Pair with resistance training to provide the mechanical stimulus that naturally upregulates MGF expression [1] . Ensure adequate protein intake (1.6–2.2 g/kg) to support tissue repair processes. Prioritize sleep and recovery; growth factor activity is enhanced during rest periods. Manage inflammation through balanced nutrition to optimize the repair environment. 13 Injection Technique General subcutaneous guidance from clinical best‑practice resources [10] . Clean the vial stopper and skin with alcohol; allow to dry. Pinch a skinfold; insert the needle at 45–90° into subcutaneous tissue [7] [11] . Do not aspirate for subcutaneous injections; inject slowly and steadily [7] . Rotate sites systematically (abdomen, thighs, upper arms) by at least 1–1.5 inches from prior sites to avoid irritation [11] . Use 23–25 gauge, 5/8‑inch needles for subcutaneous administration [7] . 14 Important Note This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. 15 References 1 PLOS ONE (2013) - Insulin‑like growth factor I (IGF‑1) Ec/Mechano Growth Factor: splice variant characterization within the growth plate View Source 2 Journal of Molecular Endocrinology (2003) - Expression of IGF‑I splice variants and structural genes in repair of rabbit tendon View Source 3 International Orthopaedics (2011) - Mechano growth factor E peptide promotes osteoblast proliferation and bone‑defect healing in rabbits View Source 4 Journal of Physiology (2003) - Mechano growth factor and other IGF‑I splice variants: expression and possible functions View Source 7 CDC (Subcut Injection PDF) - Vaccine administration: subcutaneous injection technique and site guidance View Source 8 Molecular Brain (2017) - Mechano growth factor promotes neurogenesis in the aging mouse brain View Source 9 Experimental Cell Research (2008) - MGF E‑peptide activates human muscle satellite cells View Source 10 Subcutaneous Drug Injection Review (PMC) - Pharmacologic considerations of the subcutaneous route View Source 11 Johns Hopkins Arthritis Center - How to give a subcutaneous injection (site rotation and technique) View Source 12 Pure Lab Peptides - MGF (5 mg) product page (quality and batch documentation) View Source 16 Related research, protocols, and guides Explore the available research context, protocol variants or comparisons, and practical guides. MOTS-C is a 16-amino-acid mitochondrial-derived peptide encoded within mitochondrial 12S rRNA. Laboratory studies connect it with metabolic stress signaling, AMPK activation, glucose regulation, and communication between mitochondria and the nucleus. [1] [2] Human studies have measured naturally occurring MOTS-C in blood and its response to exercise, but those observational findings do not establish a dose, injection frequency, cycle, or treatment benefit for exogenous MOTS-C. [3] [4] 06 MOTS-C 10 mg Conversion Examples A 10 mg vial contains 10,000 mcg of MOTS-C. Adding 3.0 mL produces 3,333 mcg/mL. Because a U-100 syringe holds 100 units per mL, each unit contains about 33.3 mcg. These relationships are fixed mathematical conversions; they do not establish an appropriate MOTS-C dose for a person. 200 mcg: 0.06 mL, or 6 U-100 units. 400 mcg: 0.12 mL, or 12 units. 600 mcg: 0.18 mL, or 18 units. 800 mcg: 0.24 mL, or 24 units. 1,000 mcg: 0.30 mL, or 30 units. 07 Human MOTS-C Dosage Evidence Current human research does not validate a MOTS-C injection dose. Studies have examined naturally circulating MOTS-C, associations with metabolic measures, and acute or chronic exercise responses. [4] [6] [7] [8] Those designs cannot be converted into a subcutaneous dosage protocol. Searches of clinics, forums, and community discussions also reveal conflicting schedules rather than a reliable consensus, so those anecdotes were used only for private editorial context and are not cited as evidence. 08 Storage Instructions Storage depends on the actual formulation and supplier documentation. Before reconstitution: Keep the sealed lyophilized vial dry, protected from light, and at the temperature specified on its label. After reconstitution: Refrigerate at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F) and protect from light. Discard date: Follow the formulation-specific label or laboratory stability documentation. A vial strength alone cannot establish a universal beyond-use period. Handling: Avoid vigorous shaking and unnecessary temperature cycling. 09 How the MOTS-C Peptide Works: AMPK, Metabolic Health, and Insulin Sensitivity MOTS-C is translated from a short open reading frame within mitochondrial DNA and functions as a mitochondrial-derived signaling peptide. In cell and animal models, MOTS-C responds to metabolic stress and influences the folate and purine pathways, producing AICAR accumulation and AMPK activation. [1] AMPK is a cellular energy sensor that helps coordinate glucose uptake, lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial function when energy availability changes. Laboratory work also shows that MOTS-C can move into the nucleus during metabolic stress and interact with adaptive stress-response transcriptional programs. [2] This mitochondria-to-nucleus communication is one reason MOTS-C research spans metabolic health, cellular energy, skeletal muscle, insulin sensitivity, aging, and longevity. These mechanisms are biologically interesting, but a molecular pathway is not proof that an exogenous MOTS-C injection produces a clinical benefit. 10 MOTS-C, Skeletal Muscle, Exercise, and Body Composition Research Exercise research is frequently cited in discussions of MOTS-C dosage, but it answers a different question. Reynolds and colleagues reported that MOTS-C enhanced physical performance in mice and that exercise increased endogenous MOTS-C expression in human skeletal muscle and circulation. [3] A separate human study observed changes in circulating MOTS-C after acute endurance exercise. [4] Research in endurance-trained athletes has also examined associations between chronic training and plasma MOTS-C levels. [7] These findings support MOTS-C as an exercise-responsive mitochondrial peptide, not as an exercise replacement or a validated peptide therapy. A blood-level response to exercise does not reveal how many milligrams of exogenous MOTS-C should be administered, how often it should be used, or whether a subcutaneous MOTS-C dosage is safe. 11 MOTS-C Research Evidence by Study Type The strength of a MOTS-C claim depends on the study population and outcome. The research base includes several distinct layers: Cell and molecular studies: Establish proposed AMPK, nuclear-translocation, and metabolic-stress pathways. [1] [2] Animal intervention studies: Report metabolic, exercise, ovarian, pancreatic-islet, immune, bone, cardiovascular, and skeletal-muscle findings in experimental models. [3] [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] [14] Human observational studies: Measure naturally occurring MOTS-C and examine associations with exercise or metabolic markers. [4] [6] [7] [8] Human dosing evidence: The FDA’s 2026 technical review states that human exposure data for MOTS-C drug products were not identified. [15] A 2023 review describes a broad experimental literature around metabolic homeostasis, stress, and aging, while a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis summarizes human circulating MOTS-C findings. [5] [6] Neither source establishes a standardized MOTS-C dosage protocol. 12 MOTS-C Peptide Therapy Claims, Injection Safety, and Regulatory Limits Exogenous MOTS-C is investigational and is not FDA-approved. The FDA technical review identifies important uncertainties, including the absence of identified human exposure data, the potential for immunogenicity, and difficulty characterizing peptide-related impurities. [15] That means a reliable human side-effect rate, therapeutic window, maximum dose, interaction profile, and long-term safety record have not been established. Preclinical benefits cannot be assumed to occur in humans. Circulating MOTS-C levels are biomarkers, not dosing targets. Results for a modified analog cannot be transferred automatically to native MOTS-C. Purity, formulation, sterility, and storage can materially affect experimental risk. Community-reported reactions and schedules are inconsistent and do not substitute for controlled safety data. 13 Why MOTS-C Dose and Protocol Claims Conflict Public descriptions of MOTS-C administration vary substantially. Some describe a daily protocol, while others describe one, two, or three times per week. Amounts per injection, cycle length, and timing also differ. That variation is evidence of uncertainty, not proof that several standardized MOTS-C protocols exist. No controlled human trial has established a standard protocol, a longevity protocol, or an optimal MOTS-C dose. The worked sequence on this page is intentionally limited to vial concentration, units per injection, and supply math. It should not be used to infer that people treated with MOTS-C in clinical research received these amounts. Searches of anecdotal material also surfaced both favorable and negative reports, including reports of no noticeable effect, fatigue, skin reactions, and palpitations. Those accounts are not verified safety data and are not cited publicly, but they reinforce why community claims should not be converted into recommendations. 14 Potential Benefits of MOTS-C in Preclinical Research The most frequently discussed metabolic benefits come from cell and animal experiments. In those models, MOTS-C improves aspects of glucose handling, insulin sensitivity, exercise performance, adipose homeostasis, and cellular energy regulation. [1] [3] [11] Other studies examine pancreatic-islet aging, autoimmune diabetes, bone metabolism, cardiovascular biology, and skeletal-muscle bioenergetics. [9] [10] [12] [13] [14] These experiments help explain which metabolic pathways MOTS-C targets and why the peptide is being studied. They do not prove weight loss, improved body composition, better performance, or longevity in humans. Claims that MOTS-C helps achieve those outcomes remain unconfirmed until controlled human studies test exogenous MOTS-C directly. 15 MOTS-C and Metformin: A Mechanistic Comparison, Not Equivalence MOTS-C and metformin are sometimes discussed together because both can intersect with AMPK-related metabolic signaling. The comparison is mechanistic only. It does not mean that MOTS-C acts like a clinically interchangeable medicine, produces the same effects, or has a known dose relationship with metformin. Metformin has extensive human clinical evidence; exogenous MOTS-C does not. The shared pathway should therefore be described as a research connection rather than a treatment comparison. 16 MOTS-C Dosage Questions Is there an established human MOTS-C dosage? No. Published human studies have measured endogenous MOTS-C, while the FDA reports that it has not identified human exposure data for MOTS-C drug products by any route. [4] [15] How much MOTS-C is in one U-100 unit after adding 3 mL? A 10 mg vial diluted to 3.0 mL contains 3.33 mg/mL. One U-100 unit equals 0.01 mL, so one unit contains approximately 0.0333 mg, or 33.3 mcg . Why does this MOTS-C dosage chart show 200 to 1,000 mcg? Those rows provide a consistent worked example for translating peptide mass into U-100 syringe markings and for calculating supplies. They are not derived from a human trial and should not be described as a standard, recommended, or clinically validated MOTS-C dose. Does a 10 mg vial change the underlying MOTS-C research? No. Vial strength changes concentration, units per injection, total vial use, and supply math. It does not change the compound’s evidence base. The separate 5 mg, 20 mg, and 40 mg pages exist because their reconstitution and syringe conversions differ. Does exercise research validate injected MOTS-C? No. Exercise studies show that endogenous MOTS-C levels or expression can respond to physical activity. [3] [4] They do not establish the safety or efficacy of exogenous MOTS-C administration. 17 References 1 Cell Metabolism (2015) - The mitochondrial-derived peptide MOTS-c promotes metabolic homeostasis and reduces obesity and insulin resistance (Lee C, Zeng J, Drew BG, et al.) MOTS-c is a 16–amino-acid mitochondrial-derived peptide (MDP) that acts as a metabolic regulator, primarily through AMPK activation [1] [2] . Preclinical studies show it enhances insulin sensitivity, promotes fat oxidation, improves exercise capacity, and counters age-related metabolic decline [1] [3] . No clinical trials have been completed in humans to date [12] . This educational protocol presents a once-daily subcutaneous approach with gradual titration. 06 MOTS-C 20 mg Vial and Research Context A MOTS-C 20 mg vial identifies the total peptide mass in the container. It does not establish an amount per administration. On this page, adding 3.0 mL of bacteriostatic water produces a calculated concentration of about 6.67 mg/mL. That concentration is the basis for the U-100 syringe conversions in the dosage chart, while the displayed schedule remains labeled as community-reported use. Vial contents: 20 mg MOTS-C, or 20,000 mcg total. Final volume: 3.0 mL after the page’s documented preparation. Calculated concentration: 20 mg ÷ 3.0 mL = 6.6667 mg/mL. U-100 conversion: 0.01 mL per syringe unit = about 66.7 mcg per unit. Evidence boundary: FDA’s technical review found no human exposure data for compounded MOTS-C drug products, so the vial calculation must not be mistaken for a clinically validated injection regimen. [12] The strength-specific product page documents the 20 mg vial identity and supplier destination; it is product provenance, not clinical evidence. [16] 07 MOTS-C 20 mg Concentration and U-100 Math The conversion begins with the unrounded concentration. A 20 mg vial contains 20,000 mcg. Dividing 20,000 mcg by 3.0 mL gives 6,666.7 mcg/mL. Because one U-100 unit is 0.01 mL, each unit contains approximately 66.7 mcg at this preparation. They do not add a new phase, amount, route, frequency, or duration. 08 What the 20 mg Vial Strength Changes Vial strength changes preparation math and theoretical yield. It does not, by itself, determine an appropriate research amount. For the preparation on this page, 20 mg divided across 3.0 mL creates a different concentration from other MOTS-C vial strengths, so the same liquid volume cannot be assumed to contain the same peptide mass. Concentration changes: the mass per mL depends on both vial contents and final liquid volume. Syringe markings change: U-100 units are volume markings, so they must be recalculated from the concentration. Vial yield changes: a larger vial can contain more calculated administrations at the same mass, but handling loss and product-specific limits still matter. Evidence does not change: increasing vial mass does not create human dosing evidence or establish safety, effectiveness, or product stability. [12] 09 MOTS-C and Mitochondrial Signaling MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid mitochondrial-derived peptide encoded within mitochondrial 12S rRNA. Early laboratory work connected it with metabolic homeostasis, glucose handling, and resistance to diet-induced metabolic stress in mice. [1] Later reviews describe MOTS-c as part of mitochondrial-to-nuclear communication, with proposed links to AMPK signaling, cellular stress responses, and energy metabolism. [2] [9] Mechanistic findings explain why researchers study the peptide, but they do not validate the community-reported syringe amounts on this page. Cell signaling, animal exposure, naturally circulating human MOTS-c, and an externally supplied research vial are different evidence categories. 10 Human MOTS-C Findings and Exercise Research Human research has mainly measured endogenous MOTS-c rather than administering a 20 mg research vial. In one study, exercise increased MOTS-c expression in skeletal muscle and circulating levels in people, while experimental administration and performance findings were studied in mice. [3] A separate acute endurance study measured changes in mitochondrial-derived peptides after exercise in human participants. [4] Reviews of mitochondrial-derived peptides and exercise describe promising associations with metabolic adaptation, aging, and muscle function, but they also note variable human findings and the need for more direct clinical research. [5] [10] These publications provide biological context. They do not establish the dose, frequency, route, escalation, or duration displayed in the community-reported chart. For a 20 mg research vial, the distinction is practical: no MOTS-C dose is clinically validated, and the effect of an exogenous MOTS-C injection cannot be inferred from exercise-linked changes in endogenous MOTS-C, circulating MOTS-C levels, or plasma MOTS-C measurements. [3] [4] 11 Preclinical MOTS-C Evidence Animal and cellular models account for much of the published MOTS-c evidence. Ovariectomized mouse research reported changes in adipose homeostasis and metabolic dysfunction. [6] Bone research has examined osteoblast and osteoclast pathways, while broader reviews summarize experimental work involving glucose metabolism, obesity, inflammation, and organ-specific effects. [7] [8] Other reviews place MOTS-c within a larger group of mitochondrial-derived peptides involved in energy metabolism and stress signaling. [9] Research on aging and a recent pancreatic islet cell study expands the list of investigated pathways, but those findings remain model-specific and do not supply a validated human injection protocol. [10] [11] Evidence type What it can address What it cannot establish Cell studies Signaling pathways and molecular responses Human vial dose, route, frequency, or safety Animal studies Model-specific metabolism, performance, and tissue effects A clinically validated human schedule Human observational exercise studies Endogenous MOTS-c levels and associations Effects of an injected 20 mg research vial Regulatory review Known data gaps and product-quality concerns A positive safety or efficacy conclusion 12 Storage, Handling, and Product Quality The page’s preparation card directs the reconstituted vial to refrigerated storage at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F), protected from light. Temperature guidance is not the same as a validated shelf life. A discard date requires product-specific labeling, formulation-specific stability evidence, or an applicable sterile-use rule. Record the compound, 6.67 mg/mL concentration, and reconstitution date on the vial. Use aseptic handling and a new sterile device for each withdrawal. Do not infer potency, sterility, or a universal use-by period from refrigeration alone. Follow the exact product documentation for storage and discard information when it is available. [16] FDA’s MOTS-c technical assessment identifies formulation, impurity, aggregation, immunogenicity, and human-exposure uncertainties that cannot be resolved by concentration math. [12] 13 Research Safety and Measurement Limits FDA reported that it had not identified human exposure data for compounded MOTS-c drug products and highlighted potential safety risks related to peptide characterization, impurities, aggregation, and immune responses. [12] That evidence ceiling should remain visible when interpreting any community-reported calculation. MOTS-C is not FDA-approved as a drug, and reported side effects from a standardized human MOTS-C protocol have not been established. Absence of human exposure data is not evidence that a research product is safe. [12] General subcutaneous injection resources describe skin preparation, site selection, device handling, and sharps disposal, but those sources do not validate MOTS-c or the schedule on this page. [13] [14] A literature review of subcutaneous administration also shows that formulation, molecule properties, tissue conditions, and injection volume can influence delivery behavior. [15] U-100 units describe liquid volume, not peptide potency or international units. Rounding should occur only after calculating from the full concentration. Cloudiness, particles, discoloration, or container damage require product-specific review rather than assumptions. Preclinical benefit claims should not be presented as established human outcomes. 14 MOTS-C 20 mg Frequently Asked Questions What is the MOTS-C dosage for a 20 mg vial? There is no FDA-approved MOTS-C dosage for a 20 mg vial. The primary chart preserves the site’s existing community-reported calculation sequence and labels it as nonclinical; the vial strength supplies concentration and measurement math, not a validated dose. [12] Does a 20 mg vial mean a 20 mg administration? No. The 20 mg label describes total vial contents. The chart converts much smaller displayed microgram amounts using the page’s 3.0 mL preparation. What concentration results from adding 3.0 mL? Twenty milligrams divided by 3.0 mL equals 6.6667 mg/mL, commonly displayed as about 6.67 mg/mL. How much MOTS-C is in one U-100 unit? At 6.6667 mg/mL, one U-100 unit, or 0.01 mL, contains about 0.0667 mg, which is 66.7 mcg. Are the displayed amounts supported by human dosing trials? No. Human studies have primarily measured naturally produced MOTS-c in exercise and aging research. [3] [4] FDA’s technical review found no human exposure data for compounded MOTS-c drug products. [12] Does a larger vial prove a longer usable storage period? No. Vial mass does not establish a discard date. Storage and use-by decisions require formulation-specific documentation and applicable sterile-handling rules. 15 Important Research Context This page separates three different questions: how to calculate a 20 mg vial concentration, what amounts appear in the existing community-reported chart, and what published research has actually tested. The arithmetic is reproducible, but it does not convert observational human findings or animal experiments into a validated human protocol. Exercise studies support interest in endogenous MOTS-c biology, not a 20 mg vial schedule. [3] [4] [5] The regulatory assessment documents unresolved human-exposure and product-quality questions. MOTS-C is a mitochondrial-derived peptide studied in cellular, animal, and human observational or exercise settings. [1] [3] [4] [6] Published human research has not established the injected community schedule shown below, so the table is presented only to make the 40 mg vial concentration and syringe-volume arithmetic transparent. 06 MOTS-C 40 mg Reconstitution and Dosage Math A 40 mg vial contains 40,000 mcg of MOTS-C. Adding 3.0 mL produces 13,333 mcg/mL. Because a U-100 syringe has 100 volume markings per mL, each unit equals 0.01 mL and contains about 133.3 mcg at this concentration. These are fixed mathematical conversions, not proof of an appropriate dose. 200 mcg: 0.015 mL, or 1.5 U-100 units. 400 mcg: 0.030 mL, or 3 units. 500 mcg: 0.0375 mL, or 3.75 units. 600 mcg: 0.045 mL, or 4.5 units. 800 mcg: 0.060 mL, or 6 units. 1,000 mcg: 0.075 mL, or 7.5 units. 07 What the 40 mg Vial Strength Changes Vial strength changes concentration, syringe markings, and nominal yield; it does not establish a different biological dosage range. At 3.0 mL, this 40 mg vial is four times as concentrated as a 10 mg vial mixed with the same volume. The vial contains a nominal 200 amounts at 200 mcg, 100 at 400 mcg, 80 at 500 mcg, 50 at 800 mcg, or 40 at 1,000 mcg. Nominal yield does not account for handling loss and must not be treated as a storage-life estimate. 08 Measurement and Rounding Checks Very small volumes can fall between syringe markings. A calculated 1.5-unit or 3.75-unit volume may be difficult to measure accurately with some devices. Confirm the actual syringe scale, never confuse U-100 volume markings with peptide international units, and independently verify the vial mass, final volume, concentration, and conversion before laboratory use. 09 Human MOTS-C Dosage Evidence and Its Limits Current human evidence does not establish a validated MOTS-C injection dosage, titration schedule, route, or treatment duration. Human studies have measured naturally circulating MOTS-C, metabolic associations, and responses to acute or repeated exercise. [4] [6] [7] [8] Those study designs do not test the community-reported injection rows displayed on this page and cannot be converted into a clinical dosing recommendation. The distinction matters for a MOTS-C 40 mg reconstitution protocol: the arithmetic can be exact even when the underlying injected regimen lacks human validation. The table therefore shows how specified microgram amounts translate into mL and U-100 markings, while the evidence summary separately explains what researchers have and have not studied. 10 Exercise Research and Circulating MOTS-C MOTS-C research includes studies of exercise biology rather than injected dosing. A 2021 study reported MOTS-c as an exercise-induced mitochondrial signal associated with physical capacity in humans, while later work examined circulating responses to acute endurance exercise. [3] [4] A 2024 human study further evaluated circulating MOTS-c in relation to exercise, and a systematic review summarized associations reported across human studies. [6] [7] These findings help explain why terms such as MOTS-C peptide, metabolic health, insulin sensitivity, exercise performance, and healthy aging appear in the research literature. They do not determine how much exogenous MOTS-C should be injected or whether a 40 mg vial is suitable for a particular use. 11 How MOTS-C Is Studied in Metabolic Stress MOTS-C is encoded within mitochondrial DNA and functions as a mitochondrial-derived signaling peptide. Foundational laboratory research linked MOTS-C with metabolic homeostasis and AMPK-related energy signaling. [1] Additional work reported that metabolic stress can promote nuclear translocation and adaptive gene-expression responses. [2] Reviews describe this mitochondria-to-nucleus signaling framework and the questions it raises for metabolism, aging, and disease research. [5] Other preclinical investigations have explored pancreatic islet senescence, autoimmune diabetes models, adipose-tissue homeostasis, bone metabolism, cardiovascular biology, and skeletal muscle. [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] [14] These subjects are mechanistic or preclinical research areas. They are not evidence that a MOTS-C 40 mg vial, a specific injection amount, or the displayed community schedule produces a clinical benefit. 12 Safety, Regulatory Status, and Research Uncertainty MOTS-C is not an FDA-approved drug, and no established human injection regimen appears in the published evidence summarized here. The FDA has identified MOTS-C among bulk substances that may present significant safety risks, including concerns associated with immunogenicity and insufficient safety information. [15] Unknowns include formulation quality, sterility, pharmacokinetics, dose-response behavior, interactions, adverse events, and long-term effects. Laboratory handling does not remove those uncertainties. Use validated sterile technique, keep research records, and place used needles and syringes directly into an appropriate sharps container according to local requirements. [16] 13 Storage and Handling for a Reconstituted 40 mg Vial Before mixing, keep the sealed lyophilized vial dry, protected from light, and at the temperature stated on its product label. After reconstitution, refrigerate at 2–8 °C (35.6–46.4 °F), protect from light, avoid vigorous shaking, and minimize repeated temperature cycling. Follow formulation-specific supplier or laboratory stability documentation for any discard date. The 40 mg strength and 3.0 mL final volume cannot establish a universal beyond-use period. 14 MOTS-C Reconstitution Math: Vial Size and Water To reconstitute MOTS-C accurately, confirm the MOTS-C vial mass and intended final volume before drawing bac water. This 40 mg vial uses 3.0 mL, but a different vial strength and water volume creates a different concentration. A peptide reconstitution calculator or MOTS-C dose calculator is only as accurate as those inputs. Reconstitution math should always be checked in both directions: milligrams per mL and micrograms per U-100 unit. This step-by-step reconstitution check keeps the MOTS-C protocol calculation separate from biological dose selection: Confirm vial mass: 40 mg equals 40,000 mcg per vial. Confirm final volume: 3.0 mL of bacteriostatic water is the calculation basis. Calculate concentration: 40 mg ÷ 3.0 mL = 13.33 mg/mL. Calculate syringe content: 0.01 mL per U-100 unit × 13.33 mg/mL = about 133.3 mcg per unit. Recheck the requested amount: divide the specified microgram amount by 133.3 mcg per unit. Community pages sometimes describe a MOTS-C cycle, weekly dosing, or a number of times per week. Those labels do not create human dosage evidence. This page does not validate such claims; it provides transparent MOTS-C reconstitution and MOTS-C dosage math while the human-evidence limits remain explicit. 15 MOTS-C 40 mg Dosage and Reconstitution Questions How much bacteriostatic water is used in this MOTS-C 40 mg chart? The chart uses 3.0 mL, producing about 13.33 mg/mL. A different final volume changes every syringe conversion and must be recalculated. How many mcg are in one U-100 unit? At 40 mg in 3.0 mL, one U-100 unit equals 0.01 mL and contains approximately 133.3 mcg. Does a 40 mg vial require a higher MOTS-C dosage? No. Vial strength determines total material and concentration after mixing. It does not establish the amount per administration. Is the displayed schedule clinically validated? No. It is labeled Community-reported use and is included to show calculation relationships. Published human studies have not validated this injected schedule. Can nominal vial yield determine a discard date? No. Mathematical yield and stability are different questions. Follow product-specific storage and stability documentation. 16 Important Research Note This MOTS-C 40 mg dosage protocol is an educational calculation reference. It does not provide medical advice, establish a standard of care, or recommend human consumption. Human observational and exercise findings, preclinical mechanisms, community-reported schedules, and vial-conversion arithmetic are presented as separate evidence categories so that one is not mistaken for another. 17 References 1 Cell Metabolism (2015) - The mitochondrial-derived peptide MOTS-c promotes metabolic homeostasis and reduces obesity and insulin resistance (Lee C, Zeng J, Drew BG, et al.)
